verses.text: What shall we say then? Shall we continue in sin, that grace may abound?
God forbid. How shall we, that are dead to sin, live any longer therein?
Know ye not, that so many of us as were baptized into Jesus Christ were baptized into his death?
Therefore we are buried with him by baptism into death: that like as Christ was raised up from the dead by the glory of the Father, even so we also should walk in newness of life.
For if we have been planted together in the likeness of his death, we shall be also in the likeness of his resurrection:
Knowing this, that our old man is crucified with him, that the body of sin might be destroyed, that henceforth we should not serve sin.
For he that is dead is freed from sin.
Now if we be dead with Christ, we believe that we shall also live with him:
Knowing that Christ being raised from the dead dieth no more; death hath no more dominion over him.
For in that he died, he died unto sin once: but in that he liveth, he liveth unto God.
Likewise reckon ye also yourselves to be dead indeed unto sin, but alive unto God through Jesus Christ our Lord.
Let not sin therefore reign in your mortal body, that ye should obey it in the lusts thereof.

Neither yield ye your members as instruments of unrighteousness unto sin: but yield yourselves unto God, as those that are alive from the dead, and your members as instruments of righteousness unto God.
For sin shall not have dominion over you: for ye are not under the law, but under grace.
What then? shall we sin, because we are not under the law, but under grace? God forbid.
Know ye not, that to whom ye yield yourselves servants to obey, his servants ye are to whom ye obey; whether of sin unto death, or of obedience unto righteousness?
But God be thanked, that ye were the servants of sin, but ye have obeyed from the heart that form of doctrine which was delivered you.
Being then made free from sin, ye became the servants of righteousness.

I speak after the manner of men because of the infirmity of your flesh: for as ye have yielded your members servants to uncleanness and to iniquity unto iniquity; even so now yield your members servants to righteousness unto holiness.
For when ye were the servants of sin, ye were free from righteousness.
What fruit had ye then in those things whereof ye are now ashamed? for the end of those things is death.
But now being made free from sin, and become servants to God, ye have your fruit unto holiness, and the end everlasting life.
For the wages of sin is death; but the gift of God is eternal life through Jesus Christ our Lord.

chapters.summary: Paul answers the objection his own gospel invites. If grace abounds where sin abounds, then "Shall we continue in sin, that grace may abound?" His reply is not an argument about consequences but about identity: "God forbid. How shall we, that are dead to sin, live any longer therein?" The ground of that death is baptism, and Paul appeals to it as something the Romans already know: "Know ye not, that so many of us as were baptized into Jesus Christ were baptized into his death?" The rite is not a symbol laid alongside the cross but a real joining to it — "we are buried with him by baptism into death" — and it carries the whole shape of Easter with it, so that "like as Christ was raised up from the dead by the glory of the Father, even so we also should walk in newness of life." Those united to the death are promised the resurrection: "if we have been planted together in the likeness of his death, we shall be also in the likeness of his resurrection." What died is named plainly, "our old man is crucified with him, that the body of sin might be destroyed," with the purpose stated as freedom for service, "that henceforth we should not serve sin," since "he that is dead is freed from sin." Paul then grounds the believer's security in Christ's own finished pattern: "Christ being raised from the dead dieth no more; death hath no more dominion over him," for "he died unto sin once: but in that he liveth, he liveth unto God." From this comes the chapter's hinge command, an act of the mind followed at once by acts of the body: "reckon ye also yourselves to be dead indeed unto sin, but alive unto God through Jesus Christ our Lord," then "Let not sin therefore reign in your mortal body," and "yield yourselves unto God, as those that are alive from the dead, and your members as instruments of righteousness unto God." The promise "sin shall not have dominion over you" is not license, and Paul raises the objection a second time — "shall we sin, because we are not under the law, but under grace? God forbid" — answering now with the logic of servitude: "to whom ye yield yourselves servants to obey, his servants ye are." There is no neutral ground, only "sin unto death, or of obedience unto righteousness." The Romans have changed masters, having "obeyed from the heart that form of doctrine which was delivered you," and "being then made free from sin, ye became the servants of righteousness." Paul concedes the image is homely — "I speak after the manner of men because of the infirmity of your flesh" — but presses it into a command with a direction and a destination: "yield your members servants to righteousness unto holiness." The two lives are weighed by their fruit. The old yields what "ye are now ashamed" of, and "the end of those things is death"; the new yields "fruit unto holiness, and the end everlasting life." The chapter closes on an asymmetry that refuses to make salvation a transaction: "the wages of sin is death; but the gift of God is eternal life through Jesus Christ our Lord" — death is earned, life is given.
takeaways: Paul refutes the charge that grace encourages sin not by threatening the sinner but by describing what has already happened to him. "How shall we, that are dead to sin, live any longer therein?" treats continuing in sin as incoherent rather than merely forbidden, an attempt to live a life that has already been buried.

Baptism here is not illustration but incorporation. Paul says believers "were baptized into his death" and "are buried with him," language of real union rather than resemblance, and he argues from the sacrament as an accomplished fact the Romans can be reminded of rather than persuaded into.

The chapter holds together two things easily separated: an indicative and an imperative. Believers are told to "reckon ye also yourselves to be dead indeed unto sin" — to count as true what God has done — and in the same breath to stop yielding their "members as instruments of unrighteousness." Grace is received by faith and then worked out in the body's actual members.

Freedom in Paul is never autonomy but transferred allegiance. "To whom ye yield yourselves servants to obey, his servants ye are" leaves no third option; the choice is not between service and independence but between masters, and "being then made free from sin, ye became the servants of righteousness."

The closing contrast is deliberately unbalanced. Death is called "wages," something owed and earned by the one who works for it; eternal life is called "the gift of God," never earned, always given. Holiness is commanded throughout the chapter, yet its end is never described as a paycheck.

crossRefs.label: Colossians 2:11-13 — buried with him in baptism, wherein also ye are risen with him
crossRefs.why: Paul makes the same argument in even fuller terms, adding that the burial and rising happen "through the faith of the operation of God," and that those "dead in your sins" have been "quickened together with him." Read alongside Romans 6 it shows the death-and-resurrection pattern is not a passing metaphor but Paul's settled account of what baptism effects.

crossRefs.label: Galatians 2:19-20 — I am crucified with Christ: nevertheless I live
crossRefs.why: Where Romans 6 says "our old man is crucified with him," Galatians puts the same claim in the first person and adds what fills the emptied life: "yet not I, but Christ liveth in me." It answers the question Romans 6 raises about what the new life actually consists of once the old man is dead.

crossRefs.label: Romans 7:14-25 — the good that I would I do not; but the evil which I would not, that I do
crossRefs.why: The very next movement of the letter confronts the experience that seems to contradict chapter 6, a will divided against itself even after deliverance. Read together, the two chapters keep believers from either despairing at ongoing struggle or presuming that the reckoning of verse 11 has already made obedience automatic.

crossRefs.label: Romans 8:1-14 — if ye through the Spirit do mortify the deeds of the body, ye shall live
crossRefs.why: Chapter 8 supplies the power that chapter 6 commands. The same mortification of sin's reign in the mortal body is now attributed to the indwelling Spirit, and the promise that "sin shall not have dominion over you" is grounded in "the Spirit of him that raised up Jesus from the dead" dwelling in the believer.

crossRefs.label: 1 Peter 3:18-22 — baptism doth also now save us... by the resurrection of Jesus Christ
crossRefs.why: Peter independently ties baptism to salvation and to the resurrection, and like Paul insists it is not a merely external washing but "the answer of a good conscience toward God." It corroborates the reading of Romans 6 in which the sacrament genuinely joins the believer to Christ's saving act rather than only picturing it.

crossRefs.label: Matthew 6:24 — No man can serve two masters
crossRefs.why: Jesus states the same either-or that governs the second half of Romans 6, that service is exclusive and the heart cannot be divided between rival lords. Paul's "whether of sin unto death, or of obedience unto righteousness" applies the Lord's principle to the moral life of the baptized.

interpretationNotes.claim: The Catholic tradition reads Paul's language about baptism realistically: to be "baptized into his death" and "buried with him by baptism into death" describes what the sacrament actually accomplishes, not what it depicts. Baptism is the instrument by which God joins a person to Christ's dying and rising, remits sin, and gives the "newness of life" the chapter goes on to command, which is why Paul can argue from it as an accomplished fact rather than urging his readers to make it true.

counterpoint.summary: Protestant readings divide here. Sacramental Protestants stay close to the realistic reading, holding that baptism truly conveys union with Christ where it is received in faith. Others, especially in the Reformed and Baptist streams, take the passage as describing union with Christ received by faith, with baptism as its appointed sign and seal, so that Paul addresses the baptized as believers and speaks of the sign in terms proper to the thing signified. On this reading the efficacy belongs to Christ and faith rather than to the rite itself, and the argument still holds because everyone Paul addresses has both. All sides agree that Paul is arguing from something already true of his readers, that the union with Christ's death and resurrection is real and not merely imagined, and that it grounds the moral demand that follows.

interpretationNotes.claim: Catholic teaching takes "reckon ye also yourselves to be dead indeed unto sin" as the beginning of a real transformation rather than only a change in legal standing. Baptism genuinely destroys "the body of sin" and makes the believer inwardly righteous, while concupiscence remains as an inclination to be resisted, which is why the chapter issues commands — "Let not sin therefore reign in your mortal body," "yield your members servants to righteousness unto holiness" — that assume a sanctification still underway and capable of being refused.

counterpoint.summary: Protestant interpreters typically distinguish justification, a once-for-all declaration received by faith alone, from sanctification, the lifelong process this chapter commands. On that reading "reckon" means to count as true a status already secured in Christ, and the imperatives flow out of that settled standing rather than contributing to it; the believer works from acceptance, not toward it. Both traditions insist that the freedom described is real, that the commands are genuine and binding, and that a life which persists unchanged in sin contradicts what baptism into Christ's death means.

interpretationNotes.claim: Catholic reading hears "the wages of sin is death" as concerning eternal death for sin that is grave and unrepented, not merely temporal consequence, and it takes seriously that Paul addresses this warning to baptized Christians who could still "yield" their members back to sin. The gift of eternal life remains sheer gift, but it is given into a life that must persevere, and the chapter's fruit-bearing language — "ye have your fruit unto holiness, and the end everlasting life" — describes a path that can be abandoned.

counterpoint.summary: Protestant interpreters generally read the warnings as real and searching, though many hold that those truly united to Christ will be preserved to the end, so that the exhortations function as the means by which God keeps his own rather than as evidence that salvation can be forfeited. Others within Protestantism take the warnings as genuinely conditional in much the way the Catholic reading does. All sides emphasize the deliberate asymmetry of the final verse, that death is "wages" earned while eternal life is "the gift of God," and that no reading may turn perseverance into something purchased.

verses.text: Know ye not, brethren, ( for I speak to them that know the law,) how that the law hath dominion over a man as long as he liveth?
For the woman which hath an husband is bound by the law to her husband so long as he liveth; but if the husband be dead, she is loosed from the law of her husband.

So then if, while her husband liveth, she be married to another man, she shall be called an adulteress: but if her husband be dead, she is free from that law; so that she is no adulteress, though she be married to another man.

Wherefore, my brethren, ye also are become dead to the law by the body of Christ; that ye should be married to another, even to him who is raised from the dead, that we should bring forth fruit unto God.
For when we were in the flesh, the motions of sins, which were by the law, did work in our members to bring forth fruit unto death.
But now we are delivered from the law, that being dead wherein we were held; that we should serve in newness of spirit, and not in the oldness of the letter.
What shall we say then? Is the law sin? God forbid. Nay, I had not known sin, but by the law: for I had not known lust, except the law had said, Thou shalt not covet.
But sin, taking occasion by the commandment, wrought in me all manner of concupiscence. For without the law sin was dead.
For I was alive without the law once: but when the commandment came, sin revived, and I died.
And the commandment, which was ordained to life, I found to be unto death.
For sin, taking occasion by the commandment, deceived me, and by it slew me.
Wherefore the law is holy, and the commandment holy, and just, and good.
Was then that which is good made death unto me? God forbid. But sin, that it might appear sin, working death in me by that which is good; that sin by the commandment might become exceeding sinful.
For we know that the law is spiritual: but I am carnal, sold under sin.
For that which I do I allow not: for what I would, that do I not; but what I hate, that do I.
If then I do that which I would not, I consent unto the law that it is good.
Now then it is no more I that do it, but sin that dwelleth in me.
For I know that in me ( that is, in my flesh,) dwelleth no good thing: for to will is present with me; but how to perform that which is good I find not.
For the good that I would I do not: but the evil which I would not, that I do.
Now if I do that I would not, it is no more I that do it, but sin that dwelleth in me.
I find then a law, that, when I would do good, evil is present with me.
For I delight in the law of God after the inward man:
But I see another law in my members, warring against the law of my mind, and bringing me into captivity to the law of sin which is in my members.
O wretched man that I am! who shall deliver me from the body of this death?
I thank God through Jesus Christ our Lord. So then with the mind I myself serve the law of God; but with the flesh the law of sin.

chapters.summary:
Paul argues from a case his readers already grant, since he speaks "to them that know the law": "the law hath dominion over a man as long as he liveth." A wife "is bound by the law to her husband so long as he liveth," but a death dissolves the bond, and "if her husband be dead, she is free from that law." The application is startling, because it is the believer who has died: "ye also are become dead to the law by the body of Christ; that ye should be married to another, even to him who is raised from the dead." The purpose is fruitfulness, "that we should bring forth fruit unto God" — set against the old yield, when "the motions of sins, which were by the law, did work in our members to bring forth fruit unto death." What replaces the old bondage is not lawlessness but a new mode of obedience: "that we should serve in newness of spirit, and not in the oldness of the letter."

Paul then heads off the obvious slander. "Is the law sin? God forbid." The law is the instrument of diagnosis, not the disease: "I had not known sin, but by the law: for I had not known lust, except the law had said, Thou shalt not covet." The real culprit is named and personified — "sin, taking occasion by the commandment, wrought in me all manner of concupiscence" — and the commandment that arrived as a gift became an executioner by sin's misuse: "the commandment, which was ordained to life, I found to be unto death," for "sin, taking occasion by the commandment, deceived me, and by it slew me." The verdict on the law itself is unambiguous and glowing: "the law is holy, and the commandment holy, and just, and good." Its very goodness is what exposes sin, "that sin by the commandment might become exceeding sinful."

The chapter's last movement turns from argument to anguish, spoken in the present tense and the first person. "The law is spiritual: but I am carnal, sold under sin." The speaker is divided against himself: "what I would, that do I not; but what I hate, that do I," and again, "the good that I would I do not: but the evil which I would not, that I do." That very failure vindicates the law — "I consent unto the law that it is good" — and locates the trouble deeper than the will's approval: "to will is present with me; but how to perform that which is good I find not," for "in me ( that is, in my flesh,) dwelleth no good thing." Paul describes two laws at war, "another law in my members, warring against the law of my mind," while "I delight in the law of God after the inward man." The cry that follows is not despair but appeal — "O wretched man that I am! who shall deliver me from the body of this death?" — and it is answered before the chapter closes: "I thank God through Jesus Christ our Lord." The summary line holds both halves together without resolving the tension prematurely: "with the mind I myself serve the law of God; but with the flesh the law of sin."
takeaways: Paul's marriage analogy makes freedom from the law a matter of death, not of the law's failure. It is not the commandment that dies but the believer — "ye also are become dead to the law by the body of Christ" — so that release is a remarriage "to him who is raised from the dead," and its aim is fruitfulness rather than autonomy.

The chapter is the New Testament's strongest defense of the law by the very man accused of abolishing it. Twice Paul answers an objection with "God forbid," and his verdict is that the law is "holy, and the commandment holy, and just, and good." What killed him was sin exploiting a good thing, not a defect in the thing exploited.

Sin is described as an agent, not merely an act: it "taking occasion by the commandment" deceived, slew, and now "dwelleth in me." That grammar rules out treating the divided self as an excuse. Paul never says the indwelling of sin makes him innocent — he still cries "O wretched man that I am!"

The anatomy of moral failure Paul gives is precise and uncomfortable: the problem is not ignorance of the good or even reluctance toward it, since "to will is present with me," but the gap between willing and performing — "how to perform that which is good I find not." Knowledge and good intention are shown to be insufficient without deliverance from outside the self.

The chapter ends in thanksgiving rather than in defeat. The question "who shall deliver me from the body of this death?" expects a person, not a technique, and receives one: "I thank God through Jesus Christ our Lord." The remaining tension between mind and flesh is real, but it is now carried inside gratitude.

crossRefs.label: Romans 8:1-13 — There is therefore now no condemnation to them which are in Christ Jesus
crossRefs.why: This is the answer the cry of Romans 7 reaches for, and the two chapters should never be read apart. What the law "could not do, in that it was weak through the flesh" God accomplishes in his Son, so that the righteousness of the law is "fulfilled in us, who walk not after the flesh, but after the Spirit." The struggle described in chapter 7 is neither denied nor left as the last word.

crossRefs.label: Galatians 5:16-25 — the flesh lusteth against the Spirit, and the Spirit against the flesh
crossRefs.why: Paul elsewhere describes the same internal warfare in terms that plainly concern baptized believers, saying "ye cannot do the things that ye would." That parallel is central to the dispute over who is speaking in Romans 7, since here the conflict is explicitly located within those who are told to "walk in the Spirit."

crossRefs.label: Exodus 20:1-17 — Thou shalt not covet
crossRefs.why: Paul reaches past the ritual commandments to the tenth word of the Decalogue, the one commandment that governs desire rather than deed. His choice is deliberate: a law that reaches the heart is the only law that could expose "all manner of concupiscence," which no external conformity could conceal.

crossRefs.label: Psalm 119:97-104 — O how love I thy law! it is my meditation all the day
crossRefs.why: When Paul says "I delight in the law of God after the inward man," he speaks the native language of Israel's piety rather than inventing a new sentiment. The psalmist's love of the commandment shows that Paul's critique of the law's power to save coexists with genuine reverence for the law's goodness.

crossRefs.label: Genesis 3:1-13 — the serpent beguiled me, and I did eat
crossRefs.why: Paul's language that sin "deceived me, and by it slew me" echoes the pattern of the first transgression, where a good command becomes the occasion of a lie and the lie brings death. Reading the chapters together suggests Paul is narrating not only his own experience but the human story of a commandment "ordained to life" turned by deception into a sentence.

crossRefs.label: Jeremiah 31:31-34 — I will put my law in their inward parts, and write it in their hearts
crossRefs.why: The promised new covenant addresses precisely the deficiency Romans 7 exposes, since the failure is not in the written commandment but in the heart that cannot perform it. Paul's contrast between serving "in newness of spirit, and not in the oldness of the letter" presumes that this interior writing has begun.

interpretationNotes.claim: The Catholic tradition characteristically reads the present-tense "I" of "the evil which I would not, that I do" as including the baptized believer, Paul himself as he writes, describing the abiding disorder of desire that remains after baptism. On this reading the guilt of original sin is truly remitted and the will is genuinely healed and freed, yet concupiscence persists as an inclination to sin and an occasion of struggle rather than as sin properly so called — which is why the same speaker can honestly say both "I delight in the law of God after the inward man" and "I am carnal, sold under sin." The divided self is therefore not evidence of an unconverted state but the ordinary condition of a soul in grace still contending with disordered appetite until glory.

counterpoint.summary: Protestant readings divide sharply among themselves here, and both branches are serious. One influential line takes the "I" as Paul's retrospective portrait of life under the law apart from Christ — the unregenerate or merely convicted person, since a man "sold under sin" and "brought into captivity" seems incompatible with the freedom announced in the next chapter, where "there is therefore now no condemnation." A second and equally traditional line, prominent in the Reformed heritage, takes the "I" as the regenerate believer and treats the chapter as the classic description of the Christian's lifelong warfare, in which the remaining corruption is genuinely sin and not merely an inclination — a point of real divergence from the Catholic account of concupiscence. Both traditions agree that the law is "holy, and the commandment holy, and just, and good," that the flesh cannot supply what the law demands, and that deliverance comes only "through Jesus Christ our Lord."

interpretationNotes.claim: Catholic interpretation resists reading "ye also are become dead to the law by the body of Christ" as the abolition of divine law as such. The death in view is death to the law's regime as an accusing power over those under sin, and the immediate purpose clause is positive and obligating — remarriage to the risen Christ "that we should bring forth fruit unto God," and service "in newness of spirit." The moral commandments retain their force and are now fulfilled interiorly by grace, so freedom from the letter is not release from obedience but the enabling of it.

counterpoint.summary: Protestant interpreters agree that Paul is not licensing lawlessness, but many place the accent differently, emphasizing that the believer's standing before God is entirely detached from law-keeping and that the law's abiding function is chiefly to reveal sin and drive the sinner to Christ. Some traditions add a continuing guiding use of the moral law for the Christian life, while others stress that the Spirit's leading, rather than the law as such, now governs. The disagreement concerns how directly the commandments continue to obligate and whether obedience is fruit alone or also formative of righteousness; both traditions hold that the fruit borne "unto God" is real and expected.

verses.text: There is therefore now no condemnation to them which are in Christ Jesus, who walk not after the flesh, but after the Spirit.
For the law of the Spirit of life in Christ Jesus hath made me free from the law of sin and death.
For what the law could not do, in that it was weak through the flesh, God sending his own Son in the likeness of sinful flesh, and for sin, condemned sin in the flesh:
That the righteousness of the law might be fulfilled in us, who walk not after the flesh, but after the Spirit.
For they that are after the flesh do mind the things of the flesh; but they that are after the Spirit the things of the Spirit.
For to be carnally minded is death; but to be spiritually minded is life and peace.
Because the carnal mind is enmity against God: for it is not subject to the law of God, neither indeed can be.
So then they that are in the flesh cannot please God.
But ye are not in the flesh, but in the Spirit, if so be that the Spirit of God dwell in you. Now if any man have not the Spirit of Christ, he is none of his.
And if Christ be in you, the body is dead because of sin; but the Spirit is life because of righteousness.
But if the Spirit of him that raised up Jesus from the dead dwell in you, he that raised up Christ from the dead shall also quicken your mortal bodies by his Spirit that dwelleth in you.
Therefore, brethren, we are debtors, not to the flesh, to live after the flesh.
For if ye live after the flesh, ye shall die: but if ye through the Spirit do mortify the deeds of the body, ye shall live.
For as many as are led by the Spirit of God, they are the sons of God.
For ye have not received the spirit of bondage again to fear; but ye have received the Spirit of adoption, whereby we cry, Abba, Father.
The Spirit itself beareth witness with our spirit, that we are the children of God:
And if children, then heirs; heirs of God, and joint-heirs with Christ; if so be that we suffer with him, that we may be also glorified together.
For I reckon that the sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the glory which shall be revealed in us.
For the earnest expectation of the creature waiteth for the manifestation of the sons of God.
For the creature was made subject to vanity, not willingly, but by reason of him who hath subjected the same in hope,
Because the creature itself also shall be delivered from the bondage of corruption into the glorious liberty of the children of God.
For we know that the whole creation groaneth and travaileth in pain together until now.
And not only they, but ourselves also, which have the firstfruits of the Spirit, even we ourselves groan within ourselves, waiting for the adoption, to wit, the redemption of our body.
For we are saved by hope: but hope that is seen is not hope: for what a man seeth, why doth he yet hope for?
But if we hope for that we see not, then do we with patience wait for it.
Likewise the Spirit also helpeth our infirmities: for we know not what we should pray for as we ought: but the Spirit itself maketh intercession for us with groanings which cannot be uttered.
And he that searcheth the hearts knoweth what is the mind of the Spirit, because he maketh intercession for the saints according to the will of God.
And we know that all things work together for good to them that love God, to them who are the called according to his purpose.
For whom he did foreknow, he also did predestinate to be conformed to the image of his Son, that he might be the firstborn among many brethren.
Moreover whom he did predestinate, them he also called: and whom he called, them he also justified: and whom he justified, them he also glorified.
What shall we then say to these things? If God be for us, who can be against us?
He that spared not his own Son, but delivered him up for us all, how shall he not with him also freely give us all things?
Who shall lay any thing to the charge of God’s elect? It is God that justifieth.
Who is he that condemneth? It is Christ that died, yea rather, that is risen again, who is even at the right hand of God, who also maketh intercession for us.
Who shall separate us from the love of Christ? shall tribulation, or distress, or persecution, or famine, or nakedness, or peril, or sword?
As it is written, For thy sake we are killed all the day long; we are accounted as sheep for the slaughter.
Nay, in all these things we are more than conquerors through him that loved us.
For I am persuaded, that neither death, nor life, nor angels, nor principalities, nor powers, nor things present, nor things to come,
Nor height, nor depth, nor any other creature, shall be able to separate us from the love of God, which is in Christ Jesus our Lord.

chapters.summary: Paul opens with the verdict that answers the anguish of the chapter before it: "There is therefore now no condemnation to them which are in Christ Jesus, who walk not after the flesh, but after the Spirit." The ground of that freedom is not human strength but "the law of the Spirit of life in Christ Jesus," because "what the law could not do, in that it was weak through the flesh," God did by "sending his own Son in the likeness of sinful flesh, and for sin," so that he "condemned sin in the flesh" and "the righteousness of the law might be fulfilled in us." He then draws a line between two whole orientations of a life: "they that are after the flesh do mind the things of the flesh; but they that are after the Spirit the things of the Spirit," and "to be carnally minded is death; but to be spiritually minded is life and peace." The carnal mind "is enmity against God: for it is not subject to the law of God, neither indeed can be," so "they that are in the flesh cannot please God." What marks the Christian is indwelling rather than agreement — "if so be that the Spirit of God dwell in you" — with a sharp test attached: "if any man have not the Spirit of Christ, he is none of his." That indwelling reaches even the body, for he who raised Jesus "shall also quicken your mortal bodies by his Spirit that dwelleth in you." The consequence is obligation, not license: "we are debtors, not to the flesh, to live after the flesh," and "if ye live after the flesh, ye shall die: but if ye through the Spirit do mortify the deeds of the body, ye shall live." The Spirit's work is naming as much as power. "Ye have not received the spirit of bondage again to fear; but ye have received the Spirit of adoption, whereby we cry, Abba, Father," and "the Spirit itself beareth witness with our spirit, that we are the children of God." Sonship then carries inheritance and a condition in one breath: "if children, then heirs; heirs of God, and joint-heirs with Christ; if so be that we suffer with him, that we may be also glorified together" — and against that inheritance "the sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the glory which shall be revealed in us." Paul widens the frame to the whole cosmos: "the whole creation groaneth and travaileth in pain together until now," having been "made subject to vanity, not willingly," and it waits for "the manifestation of the sons of God" so that it too "shall be delivered from the bondage of corruption into the glorious liberty of the children of God." Believers groan with it, for even those who "have the firstfruits of the Spirit" are still "waiting for the adoption, to wit, the redemption of our body." Because "we are saved by hope: but hope that is seen is not hope," the present posture is patient waiting. Into that weakness the Spirit comes: "we know not what we should pray for as we ought: but the Spirit itself maketh intercession for us with groanings which cannot be uttered," and he does so "according to the will of God." From there the chapter climbs. "All things work together for good to them that love God, to them who are the called according to his purpose"; "whom he did foreknow, he also did predestinate to be conformed to the image of his Son, that he might be the firstborn among many brethren"; "whom he did predestinate, them he also called: and whom he called, them he also justified: and whom he justified, them he also glorified." The close is a courtroom with every accuser removed — "If God be for us, who can be against us?", "He that spared not his own Son, but delivered him up for us all, how shall he not with him also freely give us all things?", "Who shall lay any thing to the charge of God’s elect? It is God that justifieth" — and the judge's place is held by one who "maketh intercession for us." Paul then names every candidate for separation and finds none that qualifies: not "tribulation, or distress, or persecution, or famine, or nakedness, or peril, or sword," under which "we are accounted as sheep for the slaughter" and yet "are more than conquerors through him that loved us"; not "death, nor life, nor angels, nor principalities, nor powers, nor things present, nor things to come"; not "height, nor depth, nor any other creature, shall be able to separate us from the love of God, which is in Christ Jesus our Lord."
takeaways: The chapter defines a Christian by possession rather than performance — "if so be that the Spirit of God dwell in you" — and then makes that indwelling the sole boundary line: "if any man have not the Spirit of Christ, he is none of his." Freedom from condemnation is not a legal fiction laid over an unchanged life but the presence of a new occupant who produces a new walk.

Paul never lets "no condemnation" drift into passivity. In the same breath as the indwelling he writes "if ye live after the flesh, ye shall die: but if ye through the Spirit do mortify the deeds of the body, ye shall live," and makes glory conditional in form — "if so be that we suffer with him, that we may be also glorified together." Mortification is the Spirit's work done through the believer's willing act, not instead of it.

Adoption is presented as both already given and not yet finished. Believers already "cry, Abba, Father" and already have the Spirit's inward witness, yet those same believers, holding only "the firstfruits of the Spirit," are still "waiting for the adoption, to wit, the redemption of our body." The Christian life is lived in the gap between a name conferred and a body not yet raised.

Redemption in this chapter is cosmic, not merely personal. "The creature was made subject to vanity, not willingly," and its release is tied to ours — creation "waiteth for the manifestation of the sons of God" before it enters "the glorious liberty of the children of God." Matter is not discarded in Paul's hope; it is delivered along with the bodies of the saints.

The unbreakable love of the closing verses is described entirely in terms of what comes at the believer from outside — sword, powers, height, depth, "any other creature" — while the warnings of verse 13 concern what the believer chooses from within. The chapter's confidence is aimed squarely at fear of hostile forces, not at the question of a will that turns away.

crossRefs.label: Romans 7:14-25 — O wretched man that I am! who shall deliver me from the body of this death?
crossRefs.why: Romans 8 is the direct answer to the cry that ends the previous chapter, where the law is good but the self divided and helpless. Read together, "no condemnation" is not a change of standard but the arrival of the power the law never supplied, since "what the law could not do, in that it was weak through the flesh," God accomplished in his Son.

crossRefs.label: Galatians 4:4-7 — God hath sent forth the Spirit of his Son into your hearts, crying, Abba, Father
crossRefs.why: Paul uses almost identical language to the adoption passage here, moving from bondage to sonship to inheritance by the same Spirit. The parallel confirms that "Abba, Father" is not a private feeling but the Spirit's own witness constituting the believer an heir, and it ties adoption to the sending of the Son "made of a woman, made under the law."

crossRefs.label: Ephesians 1:3-14 — having predestinated us unto the adoption of children by Jesus Christ
crossRefs.why: Ephesians sets predestination, adoption, and the Spirit as "the earnest of our inheritance" in the same sequence Romans 8 traces from foreknowledge to glorification. Both passages locate the divine purpose in Christ rather than in the individual considered alone, which shapes how the chain of verse 30 is read.

crossRefs.label: Genesis 3:17-19 — cursed is the ground for thy sake
crossRefs.why: The subjection of creation "to vanity, not willingly" points back to the ground cursed on account of human sin, which explains why the created order suffers a fate it did not choose. Paul's hope that creation will be "delivered from the bondage of corruption" is the undoing of that curse rather than the abolition of the world.

crossRefs.label: 2 Corinthians 5:1-5 — we that are in this tabernacle do groan, being burdened
crossRefs.why: Paul again describes believers groaning in the present body while possessing the Spirit as a pledge of what is coming, and again the hope is not escape from the body but its clothing with life. It clarifies that "the redemption of our body" in Romans 8 means resurrection, not release from bodily existence.

crossRefs.label: Romans 5:1-5 — tribulation worketh patience; and patience, experience; and experience, hope
crossRefs.why: The earlier chapter already joined suffering to hope and grounded that hope in "the love of God" shed abroad in the heart "by the Holy Ghost which is given unto us." Romans 8 completes the thought by naming what tribulation cannot do: it cannot "separate us from the love of God, which is in Christ Jesus our Lord."

interpretationNotes.claim: Catholic reading takes "whom he did foreknow, he also did predestinate" and the chain that follows as a real and gratuitous divine initiative — no one calls, justifies, or glorifies himself — while denying that it makes the human will a spectator. Predestination is read as ordered to a specific end named in the verse, "to be conformed to the image of his Son," and as fully compatible with the same chapter's conditions, "if ye through the Spirit do mortify the deeds of the body, ye shall live" and "if so be that we suffer with him." On this reading God's foreknowledge and eternal purpose embrace the free responses of those he moves by grace, and no one is ever predestined to sin or to loss; grace precedes, accompanies, and completes a cooperation it first makes possible.

counterpoint.summary: Reformed interpreters read verse 30 as an unbroken chain in which every person foreknown is finally glorified, so that election is unconditional and effectual, grounded in God's purpose alone and not in any foreseen response — a reading reinforced by "the carnal mind is enmity against God: for it is not subject to the law of God, neither indeed can be" and "they that are in the flesh cannot please God." Other Protestants, in the Arminian and Wesleyan line, read "foreknow" as God's prior knowledge of those who would believe and take predestination as corporate and Christ-centred, closer in effect to the Catholic account. Both traditions agree that salvation originates in God's initiative and not in human merit, and that the chapter's confidence rests on God's action rather than the believer's.

interpretationNotes.claim: Catholic reading holds that the sweeping assurance of "nothing shall be able to separate us from the love of God" is aimed at hostile powers and circumstances rather than at the believer's own free choice, and therefore does not guarantee that a justified person cannot fall. The list Paul compiles — tribulation, persecution, sword, angels, principalities, height, depth, "any other creature" — is a catalogue of external threats, and the same chapter warns believers directly that "if ye live after the flesh, ye shall die" and conditions glorification on "if so be that we suffer with him." Justification on this reading is a real interior state that can be forfeited by grave sin and restored by repentance, so the Christian holds a firm hope in God's fidelity without a guaranteed certainty about his own perseverance.

counterpoint.summary: Reformed and many evangelical interpreters read these verses as a promise of final perseverance: since it is "God that justifieth" and Christ "maketh intercession for us," no charge can stand and no genuine believer is finally lost, with the warnings of verse 13 functioning as the very means God uses to preserve his people and as tests distinguishing living faith from mere profession. Wesleyan and Anabaptist Protestants, by contrast, take the same warnings as real possibilities and stand close to the Catholic position. All sides affirm that the passage forbids anxious fear before accusers and hostile powers, and that assurance rests on Christ's intercession rather than on the believer's own strength.

interpretationNotes.claim: Catholic reading understands "that the righteousness of the law might be fulfilled in us" as genuine interior renewal, not only a verdict pronounced over an unchanged person. The preposition matters: the righteousness is fulfilled in the believer, by a Spirit who "dwell[s] in you," so that justification includes being made righteous and not merely being reckoned so. This is why the chapter can move without strain from "no condemnation" to the demand that believers "mortify the deeds of the body," and why walking "after the Spirit" describes the actual life of the justified rather than an optional sequel to justification.

counterpoint.summary: Protestant interpreters in the classical Reformation line distinguish justification, a declarative act in which Christ's righteousness is imputed to the believer, from sanctification, the Spirit's ongoing transformation, and read verse 4 as describing the latter flowing necessarily from the former — the law's demand met in Christ and then increasingly worked out in those who walk after the Spirit. They stress that the chapter's "no condemnation" is unqualified precisely because it does not depend on the believer's attained holiness. Both traditions insist that a real change of life follows and that a faith producing no walk after the Spirit is not the faith Paul describes.

verses.text: I say the truth in Christ, I lie not, my conscience also bearing me witness in the Holy Ghost,
That I have great heaviness and continual sorrow in my heart.
For I could wish that myself were accursed from Christ for my brethren, my kinsmen according to the flesh:
Who are Israelites; to whom pertaineth the adoption, and the glory, and the covenants, and the giving of the law, and the service of God, and the promises;
Whose are the fathers, and of whom as concerning the flesh Christ came, who is over all, God blessed for ever. Amen.
Not as though the word of God hath taken none effect. For they are not all Israel, which are of Israel:
Neither, because they are the seed of Abraham, are they all children: but, In Isaac shall thy seed be called.
That is, They which are the children of the flesh, these are not the children of God: but the children of the promise are counted for the seed.
For this is the word of promise, At this time will I come, and Sara shall have a son.
And not only this; but when Rebecca also had conceived by one, even by our father Isaac;
( For the children being not yet born, neither having done any good or evil, that the purpose of God according to election might stand, not of works, but of him that calleth;)
It was said unto her, The elder shall serve the younger.
As it is written, Jacob have I loved, but Esau have I hated.
What shall we say then? Is there unrighteousness with God? God forbid.
For he saith to Moses, I will have mercy on whom I will have mercy, and I will have compassion on whom I will have compassion.
So then it is not of him that willeth, nor of him that runneth, but of God that sheweth mercy.
For the scripture saith unto Pharaoh, Even for this same purpose have I raised thee up, that I might shew my power in thee, and that my name might be declared throughout all the earth.
Therefore hath he mercy on whom he will have mercy, and whom he will he hardeneth.
Thou wilt say then unto me, Why doth he yet find fault? For who hath resisted his will?
Nay but, O man, who art thou that repliest against God? Shall the thing formed say to him that formed it, Why hast thou made me thus?
Hath not the potter power over the clay, of the same lump to make one vessel unto honour, and another unto dishonour?
What if God, willing to shew his wrath, and to make his power known, endured with much longsuffering the vessels of wrath fitted to destruction:
And that he might make known the riches of his glory on the vessels of mercy, which he had afore prepared unto glory,
Even us, whom he hath called, not of the Jews only, but also of the Gentiles?
As he saith also in Osee, I will call them my people, which were not my people; and her beloved, which was not beloved.
And it shall come to pass, that in the place where it was said unto them, Ye are not my people; there shall they be called the children of the living God.
Esaias also crieth concerning Israel, Though the number of the children of Israel be as the sand of the sea, a remnant shall be saved:
For he will finish the work, and cut it short in righteousness: because a short work will the Lord make upon the earth.
And as Esaias said before, Except the Lord of Sabaoth had left us a seed, we had been as Sodoma, and been made like unto Gomorrha.
What shall we say then? That the Gentiles, which followed not after righteousness, have attained to righteousness, even the righteousness which is of faith.
But Israel, which followed after the law of righteousness, hath not attained to the law of righteousness.
Wherefore? Because they sought it not by faith, but as it were by the works of the law. For they stumbled at that stumblingstone;
As it is written, Behold, I lay in Sion a stumblingstone and rock of offence: and whosoever believeth on him shall not be ashamed.

chapters.summary: Paul opens under oath — "I say the truth in Christ, I lie not, my conscience also bearing me witness in the Holy Ghost" — because what follows will sound like an accusation against his own people, and it is instead a grief: "great heaviness and continual sorrow in my heart." So deep is it that he "could wish that myself were accursed from Christ for my brethren, my kinsmen according to the flesh," to whom belong "the adoption, and the glory, and the covenants, and the giving of the law, and the service of God, and the promises," and from whom "as concerning the flesh Christ came, who is over all, God blessed for ever." The problem is not that God's word failed but that it never ran along bloodlines: "they are not all Israel, which are of Israel," for "In Isaac shall thy seed be called," and "the children of the promise are counted for the seed." Paul presses the point past Ishmael to twins of one mother, chosen "being not yet born, neither having done any good or evil, that the purpose of God according to election might stand, not of works, but of him that calleth" — "The elder shall serve the younger," "Jacob have I loved, but Esau have I hated." To the objection "Is there unrighteousness with God?" he answers "God forbid," and grounds mercy in God's own freedom: "I will have mercy on whom I will have mercy," therefore "it is not of him that willeth, nor of him that runneth, but of God that sheweth mercy." Pharaoh is the counterweight — "Even for this same purpose have I raised thee up, that I might shew my power in thee" — leading to the hardest line in the chapter, "whom he will he hardeneth." When the reader protests "Why doth he yet find fault? For who hath resisted his will?", Paul refuses to argue on those terms: "Nay but, O man, who art thou that repliest against God?" "Hath not the potter power over the clay, of the same lump to make one vessel unto honour, and another unto dishonour?" Yet the sentence that follows is conditional and asymmetric — God "endured with much longsuffering the vessels of wrath fitted to destruction," while the vessels of mercy he "had afore prepared unto glory," "Even us, whom he hath called, not of the Jews only, but also of the Gentiles." The prophets are then read as forecasting exactly this shape: "I will call them my people, which were not my people," and "a remnant shall be saved," for "Except the Lord of Sabaoth had left us a seed, we had been as Sodoma." The chapter closes by naming the actual mechanism of the reversal, and it is not a decree but a stumble: the Gentiles "which followed not after righteousness, have attained to righteousness, even the righteousness which is of faith," while Israel "sought it not by faith, but as it were by the works of the law. For they stumbled at that stumblingstone" — Christ himself, of whom it is written "whosoever believeth on him shall not be ashamed."
takeaways: Paul's argument is bracketed by love, not cold determinism. It begins with a man willing to be "accursed from Christ" for his kinsmen and ends with an open promise to "whosoever believeth on him." Any reading of the middle that makes the beginning insincere or the ending unreal has lost the chapter's frame.

The election Paul defends is first about vocation and covenant lineage rather than the private eternal fate of individuals: the pairs he cites are Isaac and Ishmael, Jacob and Esau, patriarchs whose roles in salvation history are assigned before birth so "the purpose of God according to election might stand, not of works, but of him that calleth."

The potter passage is a rebuke of the questioner's standing, not an answer to the question — "who art thou that repliest against God?" Paul is asserting that the creature has no court in which to summon the Creator, which is a different move from explaining how mercy and responsibility fit together.

The grammar of verses 22-23 is deliberately uneven. God "endured with much longsuffering" the vessels of wrath "fitted to destruction," but the vessels of mercy he "had afore prepared unto glory." Glory is credited to God's preparation; destruction is described as a fitting God patiently bore, and no verse here says he authored it.

Verses 30-32 supply Paul's own explanation of who missed the righteousness, and it is a human failure rather than a divine exclusion: Israel "sought it not by faith, but as it were by the works of the law." The chapter's mystery of divine freedom is answered on the human side by the mystery of unbelief.

crossRefs.label: Romans 11:1-32 — Hath God cast away his people? God forbid
crossRefs.why: Romans 9 cannot be read as a finished verdict, because Paul himself continues the argument two chapters later and reverses the apparent conclusion: the hardening is "in part," it is "until the fulness of the Gentiles be come in," and God has "concluded them all in unbelief, that he might have mercy upon all." The vessels of chapter 9 are read in the light of an olive tree where branches are broken off for unbelief and can be grafted in again.

crossRefs.label: Exodus 9:12-17 — the LORD hardened the heart of Pharaoh
crossRefs.why: Paul's Pharaoh citation depends on the Exodus narrative, where the hardening is described in alternating voices: Pharaoh hardens his own heart, and the LORD hardens it. The alternation is the reason interpreters divide over whether divine hardening initiates the refusal or ratifies a refusal already made.

crossRefs.label: Malachi 1:1-5 — I loved Jacob, and I hated Esau
crossRefs.why: The line "Jacob have I loved, but Esau have I hated" is quoted from a prophet speaking centuries after both men died, and speaking about the nations descended from them rather than their souls. Reading the source shows the idiom is a Hebrew comparison of covenant preference between peoples, which is why the verse is not usually taken as a statement about Esau's personal damnation.

crossRefs.label: Jeremiah 18:1-10 — as the clay is in the potter's hand, so are ye in mine hand
crossRefs.why: The potter image Paul invokes is drawn from a prophetic scene in which the potter reworks a marred vessel and God explicitly makes his action contingent on repentance: if a nation turns from evil, he relents from the evil he thought to do. The background supplies the note of conditionality that the compressed image in Romans 9 leaves unstated.

crossRefs.label: Galatians 3:6-29 — they which are of faith, the same are the children of Abraham
crossRefs.why: Paul makes the same move there that he makes here, redefining Abraham's true offspring by promise and faith rather than by descent, and locating the whole line in Christ, the one "seed." It confirms that the phrase "they are not all Israel, which are of Israel" is about how the promise has always operated, not a novel exclusion.

crossRefs.label: Isaiah 28:16 — Behold, I lay in Zion for a foundation a stone
crossRefs.why: The chapter's last word is a prophetic promise that the very stone that trips the unbelieving is a sure foundation to the believing, closing an argument about divine sovereignty with an open invitation: "whosoever believeth on him shall not be ashamed." The stumbling and the security are the same stone met in two ways.

interpretationNotes.claim: The Catholic reading holds that the election Paul defends in the Jacob and Esau case concerns God's sovereign choice of instruments and peoples within salvation history — who carries the promise, and in what order — rather than an unconditional decree assigning individuals to heaven or hell before birth. Paul's evidence is that the choice was made "being not yet born, neither having done any good or evil," which excludes prior merit but does not by itself describe an eternal destiny; and the chapter's own conclusion locates Israel's loss in the fact that "they sought it not by faith," a culpable failure that presupposes a real capacity to have believed. On this reading grace is entirely unearned and always prior — "not of him that willeth, nor of him that runneth, but of God that sheweth mercy" — while human refusal remains genuinely the creature's own, so that God's hardening ratifies a resistance rather than manufacturing it.

counterpoint.summary: Much of the Reformed Protestant tradition reads the chapter as Paul's most explicit teaching on unconditional election of individuals to salvation. On this view the pre-natal choice, the flat statement that it is "not of works, but of him that calleth," the divine self-declaration "I will have mercy on whom I will have mercy," and above all the objection Paul anticipates — "Why doth he yet find fault? For who hath resisted his will?" — only make sense if the doctrine really does place the decision wholly on God's side; an interpretation that softens it into foreseen faith would not provoke that objection at all. The potter's right over "the same lump to make one vessel unto honour, and another unto dishonour" is then taken as Paul's deliberate refusal to resolve the tension in the creature's favor. Other Protestants, in the Arminian and Wesleyan streams, argue much as Catholics do, that the passage concerns corporate and vocational election and that God's foreknowledge of faith is compatible with grace being unmerited. Both traditions agree that salvation is sheer gift, that no one merits the initiative of grace, and that God is not unjust.

interpretationNotes.claim: Catholic interpretation reads the potter-and-clay passage as an assertion of God's incontestable right and of the creature's lack of standing to indict him, not as a doctrine of positive reprobation. The text is careful in a way often overlooked: God "endured with much longsuffering the vessels of wrath fitted to destruction," a passive description with no stated agent, while of the vessels of mercy it says he "had afore prepared unto glory." The tradition takes that asymmetry seriously — glory is God's own preparation, ruin is something he patiently tolerates — and therefore denies that God predestines anyone to sin or to damnation, holding instead that reprobation is permissive, consequent upon foreseen and freely chosen refusal.

counterpoint.summary: Reformed readers reply that the potter's freedom to make "one vessel unto honour, and another unto dishonour" out of one lump is stated of both vessels together, and that the parallel with Pharaoh — "Even for this same purpose have I raised thee up" — makes the hard case an instrument of God's declared plan rather than a mere toleration. Many nevertheless distinguish an active election from a passive passing-over, so that God actively gives grace to some and justly withholds it from others without being the author of their sin. Other Protestants read the vessel language as describing roles and outcomes rather than fixed individual destinies, noting that vessels in Scripture can be cleansed and reassigned. All sides agree the passage forbids the creature to arraign the Creator, that God does not sin or tempt, and that no one perishes unjustly.

interpretationNotes.claim: On the identity of Israel, Catholic reading takes "they are not all Israel, which are of Israel" as a statement about how the promise has always worked from within Israel's own story rather than as a transfer of the covenant away from the Jewish people. The chapter itself withholds nothing from them — "to whom pertaineth the adoption, and the glory, and the covenants, and the giving of the law, and the service of God, and the promises" — and the remnant texts Paul cites are proof that God has preserved a seed, not that he has abandoned the stock. The gathering of "not of the Jews only, but also of the Gentiles" is therefore the promise widening to its intended reach, and the tradition holds that God's gifts and call to Israel are never revoked.

counterpoint.summary: Protestant interpreters agree broadly that Paul is redefining the true Israel by promise rather than descent, and many press the point further, identifying the Church of believing Jews and Gentiles as the Israel of God and reading the remnant as its Old Testament anticipation. Some in that tradition see the covenant privileges of verses 4 and 5 as historical prerogatives fulfilled and thus transferred in Christ, while others, especially in dispensational streams, insist on a continuing distinct future for national Israel on the strength of the remnant promises Paul quotes here. Both traditions affirm that the present list of privileges is stated in the present tense, that Paul's own grief presupposes their standing still matters, and that the Gentile inclusion is the fulfillment of Israel's Scriptures rather than a substitute for them.

verses.text: Brethren, my heart’s desire and prayer to God for Israel is, that they might be saved.
For I bear them record that they have a zeal of God, but not according to knowledge.
For they being ignorant of God’s righteousness, and going about to establish their own righteousness, have not submitted themselves unto the righteousness of God.
For Christ is the end of the law for righteousness to every one that believeth.
For Moses describeth the righteousness which is of the law, That the man which doeth those things shall live by them.
But the righteousness which is of faith speaketh on this wise, Say not in thine heart, Who shall ascend into heaven? ( that is, to bring Christ down from above:)
Or, Who shall descend into the deep? ( that is, to bring up Christ again from the dead.)
But what saith it? The word is nigh thee, even in thy mouth, and in thy heart: that is, the word of faith, which we preach;
That if thou shalt confess with thy mouth the Lord Jesus, and shalt believe in thine heart that God hath raised him from the dead, thou shalt be saved.
For with the heart man believeth unto righteousness; and with the mouth confession is made unto salvation.
For the scripture saith, Whosoever believeth on him shall not be ashamed.
For there is no difference between the Jew and the Greek: for the same Lord over all is rich unto all that call upon him.
For whosoever shall call upon the name of the Lord shall be saved.
How then shall they call on him in whom they have not believed? and how shall they believe in him of whom they have not heard? and how shall they hear without a preacher?
And how shall they preach, except they be sent? as it is written, How beautiful are the feet of them that preach the gospel of peace, and bring glad tidings of good things!
But they have not all obeyed the gospel. For Esaias saith, Lord, who hath believed our report?
So then faith cometh by hearing, and hearing by the word of God.
But I say, Have they not heard? Yes verily, their sound went into all the earth, and their words unto the ends of the world.
But I say, Did not Israel know? First Moses saith, I will provoke you to jealousy by them that are no people, and by a foolish nation I will anger you.
But Esaias is very bold, and saith, I was found of them that sought me not; I was made manifest unto them that asked not after me.
But to Israel he saith, All day long I have stretched forth my hands unto a disobedient and gainsaying people.

chapters.summary: Paul opens not with an argument but with an ache: "my heart’s desire and prayer to God for Israel is, that they might be saved." What follows is a diagnosis offered by a man who loves the patient. His kinsmen "have a zeal of God, but not according to knowledge" — the failure is not indifference but misdirected fervor, for "being ignorant of God’s righteousness, and going about to establish their own righteousness," they "have not submitted themselves unto the righteousness of God." The verb is submission: righteousness is a gift to be received, not a wage to be earned, and the refusal is at root a refusal to be given to. Against this Paul sets the hinge of the chapter: "Christ is the end of the law for righteousness to every one that believeth" — end as goal and completion, the point the law was always aiming at. He then stages two voices. Moses speaks for "the righteousness which is of the law": "the man which doeth those things shall live by them." But "the righteousness which is of faith" speaks differently, and Paul puts Moses' own words from the wilderness into its mouth: "Say not in thine heart, Who shall ascend into heaven?" and "Who shall descend into the deep?" No one must storm heaven to fetch Christ down or ransack the grave to bring him up, because the Incarnation and the Resurrection have already happened. Therefore "The word is nigh thee, even in thy mouth, and in thy heart: that is, the word of faith, which we preach." Salvation is not remote and heroic; it is as close as a confession. Hence the chapter's most quoted line: "if thou shalt confess with thy mouth the Lord Jesus, and shalt believe in thine heart that God hath raised him from the dead, thou shalt be saved," balanced immediately by "with the heart man believeth unto righteousness; and with the mouth confession is made unto salvation" — inward belief and outward, bodily, public profession held together as one act, never one without the other. From this Paul draws the universal reach: "there is no difference between the Jew and the Greek: for the same Lord over all is rich unto all that call upon him," and "whosoever shall call upon the name of the Lord shall be saved." The second half of the chapter then works that promise backwards into a chain of necessity: "How then shall they call on him in whom they have not believed? and how shall they believe in him of whom they have not heard? and how shall they hear without a preacher? And how shall they preach, except they be sent?" Calling depends on believing, believing on hearing, hearing on preaching, preaching on being sent — so the gospel is not a private discovery but a commissioned mission, and its messengers wear the prophet's blessing: "How beautiful are the feet of them that preach the gospel of peace." Yet sending does not compel: "they have not all obeyed the gospel," and the prophet's complaint stands, "Lord, who hath believed our report?" Paul distills the whole sequence into a single principle: "faith cometh by hearing, and hearing by the word of God." He then closes the escape routes. Did they not hear? "Yes verily, their sound went into all the earth." Did Israel not know? Moses himself warned, "I will provoke you to jealousy by them that are no people," and Isaiah dared even more: "I was found of them that sought me not; I was made manifest unto them that asked not after me." The chapter ends not in condemnation but in a posture — God with open arms and a wounded patience: "All day long I have stretched forth my hands unto a disobedient and gainsaying people."
takeaways: Zeal is not self-validating. Paul grants his kinsmen a genuine "zeal of God" and still calls it "not according to knowledge," which means sincerity, effort, and religious seriousness can all be present while the one necessary thing — submission to "the righteousness of God" — is absent. The gravest religious error in this chapter is committed by devout people.

The failure Paul names is not lawbreaking but self-construction: "going about to establish their own righteousness." A righteousness one builds remains one's own possession and therefore cannot be received as gift; the sin is not that the effort is too small but that it is claimed rather than accepted.

"Christ is the end of the law for righteousness" reads as fulfillment rather than abolition. Paul does not discard Moses — he quotes him twice, and puts the words of the wilderness covenant into the mouth of "the righteousness which is of faith." The law's own voice testifies that the word is already "nigh thee."

Faith in this chapter is never purely interior. Heart and mouth are named together twice, and the confession is bodily, audible, and public: "with the heart man believeth unto righteousness; and with the mouth confession is made unto salvation." A faith that never surfaces in word and act is not the faith Paul describes.

The chain "call — believe — hear — preach — sent" makes salvation structurally ecclesial and missionary. Because "faith cometh by hearing, and hearing by the word of God," no one is expected to generate faith privately; God binds the gift to a word carried by messengers he sends, and the last word of the chapter is his own stretched-out hands.

crossRefs.label: Deuteronomy 30:11-14 — the word is very nigh unto thee, in thy mouth, and in thy heart
crossRefs.why: Paul lifts his "Who shall ascend into heaven?" and "The word is nigh thee" language directly from Moses' final covenant appeal, where the commandment is declared neither hidden nor far off. Reading them together shows Paul arguing that the gospel is not a break with Moses but the nearness Moses promised, now made flesh in a Christ who has already come down and already risen.

crossRefs.label: Leviticus 18:5 — which if a man do, he shall live in them
crossRefs.why: This is the text behind Paul's summary of the righteousness of the law, "That the man which doeth those things shall live by them." It supplies the contrast the whole chapter turns on: a life promised to the doer set beside a righteousness "which is of faith" that speaks of a word already near rather than a height still to be scaled.

crossRefs.label: Joel 2:32 — whosoever shall call on the name of the LORD shall be delivered
crossRefs.why: Paul's "whosoever shall call upon the name of the Lord shall be saved" is Joel's promise, spoken in a prophecy of the outpoured Spirit. By applying to Jesus a text whose Lord is the God of Israel, Paul both identifies Christ with that Lord and grounds his claim that "there is no difference between the Jew and the Greek" in Israel's own scriptures.

crossRefs.label: Isaiah 52:7 — How beautiful upon the mountains are the feet of him that bringeth good tidings
crossRefs.why: The blessing Paul pronounces on preachers comes from Isaiah's herald announcing peace and the reign of God to a city in exile. Set in Romans, it makes the ordinary work of proclamation the visible link in the chain from sending to hearing to faith, and it dignifies the messenger by the message he carries rather than by himself.

crossRefs.label: Isaiah 53:1 — Lord, who hath believed our report?
crossRefs.why: Paul answers his own triumphant chain of preaching with this lament, quoted from the opening of the Suffering Servant song. The placement is deliberate: the report that meets unbelief is precisely the report of one "wounded for our transgressions," so rejection of the gospel is shown to be an old and foretold response to a crucified righteousness.

crossRefs.label: Romans 9:30-33 — they stumbled at that stumblingstone
crossRefs.why: The verses immediately preceding this chapter state the same problem in different terms: Gentiles who did not follow after righteousness attained it by faith, while Israel, seeking it "as it were by the works of the law," stumbled. Chapter ten is the pastoral and scriptural unfolding of that stumble, and chapter eleven will insist it is not a fall beyond recovery.

interpretationNotes.claim: Catholic reading takes "if thou shalt confess with thy mouth the Lord Jesus, and shalt believe in thine heart" as describing the whole movement by which a person enters salvation, not as a self-contained formula that completes it. The pairing of heart and mouth already refuses a purely interior faith by requiring an audible, bodily profession, and the Church has always understood that this confession is normatively made and sealed in baptism, where the believer's word and God's act meet. Read alongside the chapter's own logic — a word that must be preached by those who are "sent" — the confession is the entry into a life of faith working through charity and perseverance, so that "thou shalt be saved" names a salvation begun, carried, and completed by grace rather than a transaction closed at the moment of speaking.

counterpoint.summary: Protestant interpreters read verses nine and ten as the clearest statement in scripture that salvation comes through faith in the risen Christ received personally, and they resist any reading that makes the sacrament rather than faith the instrument. On this view the mouth's confession is the natural overflow and evidence of the heart's belief, not an added condition, and the very point of the passage is its accessibility: nothing must be ascended to or descended for, since "the word is nigh thee." Many would add that baptism and a confessing life follow genuine faith rather than constituting it. Both traditions agree that the confession is no mere formula, that it must be heartfelt and public, that it is worked in a person by grace through a word that is preached, and that the one confessed is the crucified and risen Lord.

interpretationNotes.claim: Catholic reading understands "Christ is the end of the law for righteousness" as fulfillment and destination rather than abolition, and "going about to establish their own righteousness" as the condemnation of self-generated merit apart from grace, not of obedience as such. On this reading Paul's target is a righteousness claimed as one's own possession — the refusal to have "submitted themselves unto the righteousness of God" — while the works that flow from grace within the believer are God's own righteousness bearing fruit and are never in competition with it. The chapter's insistence that faith must reach the mouth is taken as a sign that saving faith is by nature active and embodied.

counterpoint.summary: Protestant interpreters generally read this section as the heart of justification by faith alone, with the righteousness of God received as an imputed gift and human works excluded entirely from its ground. They stress the sharpness of the contrast Paul draws between "the man which doeth those things shall live by them" and a righteousness "which is of faith," and would warn that any works admitted into the basis of acceptance reintroduces exactly the establishing of "their own righteousness" Paul condemns. Both traditions affirm that righteousness before God originates wholly in his gift, that Christ is the goal toward which the law pointed, and that no accumulation of religious effort can substitute for submitting to what God gives.
