verses.text: I commend unto you Phebe our sister, which is a servant of the church which is at Cenchrea:
That ye receive her in the Lord, as becometh saints, and that ye assist her in whatsoever business she hath need of you: for she hath been a succourer of many, and of myself also.
Greet Priscilla and Aquila my helpers in Christ Jesus:
Who have for my life laid down their own necks: unto whom not only I give thanks, but also all the churches of the Gentiles.
Likewise greet the church that is in their house. Salute my wellbeloved Epaenetus, who is the firstfruits of Achaia unto Christ.
Greet Mary, who bestowed much labour on us.
Salute Andronicus and Junia, my kinsmen, and my fellowprisoners, who are of note among the apostles, who also were in Christ before me.
Greet Amplias my beloved in the Lord.
Salute Urbane, our helper in Christ, and Stachys my beloved.
Salute Apelles approved in Christ. Salute them which are of Aristobulus’ household.
Salute Herodion my kinsman. Greet them that be of the household of Narcissus, which are in the Lord.
Salute Tryphena and Tryphosa, who labour in the Lord. Salute the beloved Persis, which laboured much in the Lord.
Salute Rufus chosen in the Lord, and his mother and mine.
Salute Asyncritus, Phlegon, Hermas, Patrobas, Hermes, and the brethren which are with them.
Salute Philologus, and Julia, Nereus, and his sister, and Olympas, and all the saints which are with them.
Salute one another with an holy kiss. The churches of Christ salute you.
Now I beseech you, brethren, mark them which cause divisions and offences contrary to the doctrine which ye have learned; and avoid them.
For they that are such serve not our Lord Jesus Christ, but their own belly; and by good words and fair speeches deceive the hearts of the simple.
For your obedience is come abroad unto all men. I am glad therefore on your behalf: but yet I would have you wise unto that which is good, and simple concerning evil.
And the God of peace shall bruise Satan under your feet shortly. The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with you. Amen.
Timotheus my workfellow, and Lucius, and Jason, and Sosipater, my kinsmen, salute you.
I Tertius, who wrote this epistle, salute you in the Lord.
Gaius mine host, and of the whole church, saluteth you. Erastus the chamberlain of the city saluteth you, and Quartus a brother.
The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with you all. Amen.
Now to him that is of power to stablish you according to my gospel, and the preaching of Jesus Christ, according to the revelation of the mystery, which was kept secret since the world began,
But now is made manifest, and by the scriptures of the prophets, according to the commandment of the everlasting God, made known to all nations for the obedience of faith:
To God only wise, be glory through Jesus Christ for ever. Amen.

chapters.summary: After eleven chapters of argument and four of exhortation, Paul closes the letter with names. He begins by commending "Phebe our sister, which is a servant of the church which is at Cenchrea," asking that the Romans "receive her in the Lord, as becometh saints" and "assist her in whatsoever business she hath need of you," for "she hath been a succourer of many, and of myself also." Then comes the roll: "Priscilla and Aquila my helpers in Christ Jesus," who "have for my life laid down their own necks"; "the church that is in their house"; Epaenetus, "the firstfruits of Achaia unto Christ"; "Mary, who bestowed much labour on us"; "Andronicus and Junia, my kinsmen, and my fellowprisoners, who are of note among the apostles, who also were in Christ before me"; "Tryphena and Tryphosa, who labour in the Lord" and "the beloved Persis, which laboured much in the Lord"; "Rufus chosen in the Lord, and his mother and mine." Some twenty-six people are named, whole households are addressed, and the greeting is meant to be enacted physically: "Salute one another with an holy kiss. The churches of Christ salute you." Into this warmth Paul drops a single sharp warning: "mark them which cause divisions and offences contrary to the doctrine which ye have learned; and avoid them," since such teachers "serve not our Lord Jesus Christ, but their own belly; and by good words and fair speeches deceive the hearts of the simple." His wish for them is discernment without corruption, "wise unto that which is good, and simple concerning evil," and his assurance is that "the God of peace shall bruise Satan under your feet shortly." The scribe himself breaks in — "I Tertius, who wrote this epistle, salute you in the Lord" — followed by Gaius the host and "Erastus the chamberlain of the city." The letter ends in doxology, praising "him that is of power to stablish you according to my gospel" and "the revelation of the mystery, which was kept secret since the world began, But now is made manifest, and by the scriptures of the prophets... made known to all nations for the obedience of faith: To God only wise, be glory through Jesus Christ for ever. Amen."
takeaways: The heaviest doctrinal letter in the New Testament ends in a list of names, and that is not an accident of form. Righteousness by faith is shown landing in actual households — "the church that is in their house" — among people known by nickname, kinship, and what they suffered, so that doctrine is never abstract from the community it creates.

The labour of the gospel in this chapter is conspicuously shared by women. Phebe is "a servant of the church" entrusted with "business" among the Romans, Priscilla is named before her husband as a fellow "helper in Christ Jesus," Mary "bestowed much labour," Tryphena, Tryphosa, and Persis "labour in the Lord," and Junia is "of note among the apostles." Paul uses the same working vocabulary for them that he uses for himself.

The one command in an otherwise affectionate chapter is a command of separation: "mark them which cause divisions and offences contrary to the doctrine which ye have learned; and avoid them." The test given is not eloquence but appetite and effect — such men "serve not our Lord Jesus Christ, but their own belly" and "by good words and fair speeches deceive the hearts of the simple."

Paul's prayer that they be "wise unto that which is good, and simple concerning evil" refuses both naivety and worldly cunning. Christian discernment is meant to be expert in what is good and deliberately inexperienced in what is not, which is the exact reversal of the wisdom Eden offered.

The closing doxology gathers the whole letter into one word: the "mystery, which was kept secret since the world began, But now is made manifest." The gospel is presented as neither novelty nor secret knowledge, since it is attested "by the scriptures of the prophets" and published "to all nations for the obedience of faith" — faith that obeys, not faith set against obedience.

crossRefs.label: Acts 18 — Aquila... with his wife Priscilla... expounded unto him the way of God more perfectly
crossRefs.why: Luke supplies the history behind Paul's greeting: the tentmaking couple who hosted him at Corinth, sailed with him from Cenchrea, and privately instructed the eloquent Apollos. Reading the two texts together shows that the "helpers in Christ Jesus" of Romans 16 were catechists and hosts of a house church, not merely donors.

crossRefs.label: Genesis 3:15 — it shall bruise thy head, and thou shalt bruise his heel
crossRefs.why: Paul's promise that "the God of peace shall bruise Satan under your feet shortly" deliberately echoes the sentence spoken over the serpent in Eden. The crushing promised to the woman's seed is extended to the Church, so that the believers at Rome share in a victory already won rather than waiting for one still in doubt.

crossRefs.label: 1 Timothy 3:8-13 — Likewise must the deacons be grave... Even so must their wives be grave
crossRefs.why: The pastoral instructions on deacons stand behind the question of what Paul means in calling Phebe "a servant of the church which is at Cenchrea," since the same word family is used for an office and for ordinary service. The passage frames the long debate over whether Phebe holds a recognized ministry or is being praised for generous help.

crossRefs.label: Ephesians 3:3-11 — by revelation he made known unto me the mystery
crossRefs.why: The doxology's "revelation of the mystery, which was kept secret since the world began, But now is made manifest" is the same theme worked out at length elsewhere: a plan hidden in God and now disclosed, whose content is that the Gentiles are fellow heirs. Both passages insist the mystery is public preaching, not private gnosis.

crossRefs.label: Romans 1:1-6 — for obedience to the faith among all nations
crossRefs.why: The letter's last line, "made known to all nations for the obedience of faith," repeats almost word for word the purpose stated in its first paragraph. Romans is bracketed by the same phrase, showing that everything argued in between serves a faith that issues in obedience among the nations.

crossRefs.label: Philippians 3:18-19 — whose God is their belly, and whose glory is in their shame
crossRefs.why: Paul uses the identical diagnosis of false teachers there as here, where they "serve not our Lord Jesus Christ, but their own belly." The parallel confirms that his objection is not to disagreement as such but to a self-serving appetite dressed in "good words and fair speeches."

interpretationNotes.claim: Catholic reading takes the ministries named here as genuinely ecclesial and not merely informal: Phebe is "a servant of the church which is at Cenchrea," an office-bearing description attached to a particular local church and carrying a commission the Romans are told to honor, and the ancient order of deaconesses is understood as a real ministry of the early Church. At the same time the tradition distinguishes this diaconal and apostolic labour from the ministerial priesthood, holding that the greetings show women exercising substantial, publicly recognized ministry — hosting churches, instructing, travelling as trusted envoys, being "of note among the apostles" — without thereby establishing that they exercised the sacramental office of presbyter or bishop.

counterpoint.summary: Protestant readings divide among themselves over this chapter. Egalitarian interpreters press the plain force of the words: Phebe is given the same title used for recognized deacons, Junia is naturally read as a woman who is "of note among the apostles," and Priscilla is named before Aquila and elsewhere teaches a preacher, which together suggest the earliest churches recognized women in leading and teaching roles that later structures narrowed. Complementarian interpreters answer that the vocabulary here is descriptive rather than official — "servant" and "helpers" and "labour in the Lord" are Paul's ordinary words for any co-worker — that being "of note among the apostles" may mean well regarded by the apostles rather than counted among them, and that greetings are too slender a base on which to build church order against clearer instructions elsewhere. Both traditions agree that Romans 16 shows women doing indispensable, risky, and publicly honored work for the gospel.

interpretationNotes.claim: In the Catholic reading, "mark them which cause divisions and offences contrary to the doctrine which ye have learned; and avoid them" presupposes an already-received, publicly identifiable body of teaching handed on to the Roman church, which none of them founded and which Paul had not yet visited. The standard by which divisive teachers are recognized is therefore "the doctrine which ye have learned" — apostolic teaching held in common by the churches — so the verse is read as supporting a living rule of faith carried by the Church's ordinary transmission, with authority to discern and exclude.

counterpoint.summary: Protestant interpreters agree that Paul appeals to a fixed deposit of teaching received before he wrote, and that a community may and must separate from those who contradict it. They generally identify that deposit with the apostolic gospel now inscribed in Scripture rather than with an ongoing magisterial office, noting that Paul's own test in the next verse is moral and doctrinal rather than jurisdictional — such men "serve not our Lord Jesus Christ, but their own belly" and deceive "by good words and fair speeches." Both traditions affirm that the gospel Paul preached is objective and normative, that it was delivered before it was written down, and that the Church has a duty to mark and avoid teaching that contradicts it.
